BioPharmCatalyst small-molecule pricing analysis

Cumulative abnormal return (CAR, T-2..T+2 vs. XBI) around FDA Approved or CRL (Complete Response Letter) catalysts, small-molecule/peptide drugs only, filtered from the BioPharmCatalyst scrape (Tejas1415/Web-Scrape-Stock-Ticker-and-Company-Name-Datasets).

Coverage caveats, read before using these numbers: the source file covers 2009-07-05 to 2020-01-14 only — not the trailing 10 years as originally hoped; it is a static scrape, stale by ~6 years. Of 462 unique small-molecule/peptide Approved-or-CRL events (363 rows after PubChem filtering), 249 (68.6%) have priceable Yahoo Finance history — the other 114 fail because 55 tickers were delisted/acquired long enough ago that Yahoo has purged their price history entirely (e.g. ARNA, CLVS, SGEN, MYL, AGN — all real M&A exits), not because of a pipeline bug.

Headline result

CAR window is T-2..T+2 (2 trading days each side of the catalyst date), market-model-adjusted vs XBI, same estimator as the CTOD/EDGAR notebook's short_window_car(). Alpha/beta are fit on an earnings-trimmed estimation window (estimation-window days beyond ±3σ dropped before the fit, ~1.7 days/event); this is now the primary estimator. It moved the numbers by ~0.3pp vs untrimmed, i.e. immaterially. See the long-window section for the ±1yr raw-price shape.

Two-sample test (do Approved and CRL react differently from each other?): Mann-Whitney U p = 1.5e-8, Welch t-test p = 5.4e-6 — both far past conventional significance (0.05), on real sample sizes (not the n=10-83 the EDGAR-matched pipeline was stuck at). One-sample tests (does each group react differently from zero?) tell the more precise story: Approved is not significant vs. zero (Wilcoxon p=0.12) — the market treats approval as expected/priced-in, not news. CRL is highly significant vs. zero (Wilcoxon p=1.9e-6) — a CRL is the real information shock. This is the same asymmetry the CTOD/EDGAR track found for Phase 3 Success vs. Failure.

Median vs mean matters for a backtest. The tiles above lead with the median (robust summary), but a strategy captures the mean over many trades. The CRL mean (−19.1%) is far below its median (−11.2%) — a left-skewed tail of catastrophic drops. For any P&L/backtest use the mean and the full distribution, not the median; the median under-states the failure-side payoff (and the per-trade variance is large, std ≈ 24%).

Excluding big pharma (dropping the 18 diversified large-caps like PFE/JNJ/NVS, where one drug is a tiny fraction of firm value): the effect gets stronger, not weaker — CRL n=28 median −22.1% (mean −26.7%), Approved-vs-CRL Mann-Whitney p=9.7e-9. So the signal is a small-cap phenomenon and is not being driven by the big names.

CAAR path: where the move actually happens

This is the "AR and CAR together" view you asked about. Each point is the cumulative average abnormal return up to that trading day; the slope between two points is that day's average abnormal return. Reading it: a line climbing steadily = the stock gains a bit almost every day (a drift); a line flat-then-jump = nothing until a one-day shock. Shaded band = the tight T-2..T+2 window used for the significance tests above.

This explains why Approved looks "not significant" in the tight window. Approved (green) drifts up gradually from about T-30 (+0.2%) to T0 (+3.1%) — only +0.7% of that lands on the event day itself. The market is pricing the approval in over the weeks before, consistent with anticipation / information leakage (your "heard the rumor" read). A 5-day window centered on T0 catches only the small tail of a move that already mostly happened, so it reads as non-significant — the move is diffuse, not absent. CRL (red) is the opposite: flat until T-1, then −10% in a single day at T0 — a genuine surprise the tight window captures fully. If you want Approved significance, widen the window to roughly T-20..T+2 (captures the run-up); but note that a wider pre-window also starts absorbing unrelated news, so treat "approval is anticipated" as the finding rather than something to engineer away.

Zooming out to 6 months refines the story. This longer path uses the market-adjusted return (stock − XBI) instead of the market model — over ~126 trading days a fitted alpha would compound into drift, and a 6-month pre-window would overlap the estimation window, so beta=1/alpha=0 is the robust long-horizon choice (deliberately a different estimator from the 30-day chart above). Reading it: Approved (green) is essentially flat for the first ~5 months and only lifts to about +5% in the final ~20-30 trading days — so the anticipation is a last-month effect, not a slow six-month drift. CRL (red) wanders up to ~+6% mid-window then back to zero before the one-day crash at T0 — no clean early-warning signal, just the surprise. Practical read: the tradeable Approved run-up window is roughly the last month before the decision, not earlier.

Robustness: earnings-day trimming

Check that an earnings day inside the 120-day estimation window isn't distorting the fitted alpha/beta (and therefore the CAR). Re-fit dropping any estimation-window day beyond ±3σ (earnings/news proxy; ~1.7 days dropped per event), then recompute. Result: negligible. Median CAR change 0.31pp; Approved-vs-CRL Mann-Whitney p goes 5.4e-8 → 1.5e-8 (if anything slightly stronger). The headline is not an artifact of estimation-window contamination.

Reading this as Step 1 of a strategy (prediction assumed)

This pricing study measures the payoff per outcome; Steps 2-4 assume a model can predict the outcome. Under that premise:

  • All the P&L is on the failure side. Even a perfect model earns ~0 on approvals (median +0.3%, priced in). The strategy reduces to: short predicted failures, do nothing on approvals.
  • Optimize for the rare class. What matters is precision/recall on the ~16% failure class, not headline accuracy — a model strong on approvals but weak on failures is worthless here.
  • Favorable skew. Approval ≈ 0, CRL mean ≈ −19% (−27% small-cap): small give-up when wrong, large gain when right.
  • Still binding even with a perfect model: thin capacity (~3.6 CRLs/yr), small-cap borrow/liquidity, elevated PDUFA option premium, and survivorship (31% of events dropped, disproportionately dead companies).

Self-critique: how this analysis could mislead

Issues in the method itself, independent of the trading question — worth fixing before these numbers carry weight.

  • Median hides the payoff; mean is what you capture. CRL median −11.2% but mean −19.1% (small-cap mean −26.7%). A backtest earns the mean over many trades. Leading with the median under-states the failure payoff and hides the fat left tail. Report mean + full distribution + bootstrap CI for anything downstream.
  • Events are not independent, so the p-values are optimistic. 33 drug/ticker pairs contribute multiple events (76 of 249 rows); one ticker has 20. Repeated readouts of the same drug/company are correlated draws — effective n is below 40 on the CRL side. Quantified in the next section — collapsing to one observation per drug (and per company) weakens the p-values as expected but the effect survives.
  • Multiple comparisons. We have now sliced n=40 CRLs many ways (windows T-1..T-5, big-pharma splits, yearly, trimmed vs untrimmed). Treat the direction as robust; do not over-read any single p-value — some significance is expected by chance across this many cuts.
  • Survivorship bias in the sample construction. Dropping 114/363 events for missing Yahoo history removes exactly the worst outcomes (delisted/acquired-after-failure). This biases the measured CRL payoff toward the survivors and understates true tail risk. Needs an explicit missing-name audit, same gap as the CTOD track.
  • Benchmark model may be wrong for micro-caps. Beta is fit vs XBI (large/mid biotech). A micro-cap's true risk model is closer to IWM/XBI-small; a mis-specified beta leaks into the abnormal return. Worth a sensitivity check with an alternate benchmark.
  • Outcome-conditioned by construction. Bucketing by realized Approved/CRL and reporting the reaction is correct for measuring an archetype (Step 1), but it is not a signal on its own — it only becomes tradeable when paired with the prediction model. Keep that boundary explicit so the reaction size is never mistaken for standalone alpha.

Robustness: correcting for non-independent events

The tests above count all 249 events as independent draws, but the same drug/company often appears more than once (e.g. a drug that gets a CRL twice before approval). Those repeats are correlated, which inflates significance. Below, each row collapses repeat readouts into a single observation (the mean CAR of that drug's / company's events of the same outcome) and re-runs the tests — a stricter, honest count.

Sample definitionCRL nCRL medianCRL mean CRL vs 0 (p)Appr-vs-CRL (p)
All events (as used above)40−11.2%−19.1%1.9e-61.5e-8
One obs per drug+company+outcome31−7.6%−14.2%1.3e-43.9e-6
One obs per company+outcome (strictest)28−9.1%−15.8%4.8e-53.2e-5

Read: deduplicating drops the CRL count from 40 to 28-31 and weakens the p-values by roughly two orders of magnitude — exactly what you'd expect when you stop over-counting correlated events. But even in the strictest one-per-company version the CRL reaction is still highly significant vs zero (p=4.8e-5) and vs Approved (p=3.2e-5), median around −8 to −9%. The result is not an artifact of a handful of multiply-counted drugs (Iluvien, Tlando, Sustol, etc.). Note the median shrinks (−11% → −8%) because several of the most extreme drops were the repeat CRLs now merged — a sign the raw sample was somewhat flattered by them, which is precisely why this check matters.

Backtest: perfect-foresight strategy ($10M, 2016-2019)

Step 2 — a perfect-foresight ceiling, then the realistic-model haircut. Window 2016-2019, 320 small-cap events = 217 successes + 103 failures, capped pre-COVID (2020-02-14). The deployed book is long+lend (the short leg was tested and dropped — see below). Constraints that bind are built in: small-cap only, per-name/gross caps, XBI beta-hedge, and costs.

The perfect-foresight ceiling (100% model) is $28.9M / 29% / Sharpe 1.65 / −16%. The headline above is the honest 90%-accurate-model result; at 80% ~$24M.

Why 2016-2019: those 4 years hold ~95% of the tradeable events. 217 successes vs 103 failures (~2:1) — the deployed book is the 217 long+lend names.

The strategy, leg by leg (with a worked $1M example)

Every position is beta-hedged: its return is measured as stock_return − beta × XBI_return, so we strip out biotech-market direction and keep only the event's own move. The two earning legs:

LEG 1 — LONG + LEND  (a predicted success)

Buy at T−20, hold to T+63, and lend the shares to the crowd shorting it. You earn the price rise plus the borrow fee.

LONG P&L = price move + lending income − cost
  price = notional × (beta-hedged return, T−20→T+63)
  lending = notional × rate × util × [20/252×1.0 + 63/252×0.10]
  cost = notional × 85 bps

example, $1M, +5% move, rate 100%/yr, util 40%:
  price = 1,000,000 × 5% = +$50,000
  lending = 31,700 (pre) + 10,000 (post) = +$41,700
  cost = −$8,500
  LONG net = +$83,200 (8.3% on $1M)

LEG 2 — SHORT  (a predicted failure)

Short (or buy puts) at T−10, cover at T+5 — capture the one-day crash. You pay a borrow fee to hold the short. Only ~60% are executable (the biggest-drop names are un-borrowable — skipped).

SHORT P&L = −(price move) − borrow cost − cost
  price move = notional × (beta-hedged return, T−10→T+5) [negative]
  borrow cost = notional × rate × (15/252)
  cost = notional × 85 bps

example, $1M, −12% crash (a shortable one), borrow 100%/yr:
  gain = 1,000,000 × 12% = +$120,000
  borrow = 1M × 15/252 = −$59,500
  cost = −$8,500
  SHORT net = +$52,000 — but $0 the ~40% you can't borrow

P&L by leg, per scenario (100% model, so columns differ only by the cost assumptions — this is the proof the short leg does not pay):

Scenario (assumptions)Long priceLong lendShort netFrictGross
BEAR — borrow 30%, 30% short, 150bps+$15.2M+$0.6M−$1.6M−$1.8M+$12.3M
BASE — borrow 100%, 60% short, 80bps+$14.7M+$4.3M−$0.6M−$1.1M+$17.3M
BULL — borrow 200%, 70% short, 50bps+$14.7M+$17.4M+$0.1M−$0.8M+$31.5M

Short is negative in BEAR (−$1.6M) and BASE (−$0.6M), positive only in BULL. Of 103 failures only ~60% (62) are borrowable — the biggest drops are un-borrowable — so what is left barely covers borrow cost. It also does nothing for neutrality (the XBI hedge does that). So it is dropped; deployed = long+lend. Long price is stable (~$15M); lending is the swing factor ($0.6M → $4.3M → $17.4M), and adds +18% over price-only ($24.6M → $28.9M at 100% model).

Does the XBI hedge help? Hedged $28.9M / Sharpe 1.65 / −16% vs un-hedged $33.8M / 1.78 / −14% — un-hedged won on every metric here, but only because biotech had no sustained sector crash in this window (XBI's own −36% shows it can). The hedge is insurance that didn't pay in-sample (mandate / tail), not a return driver.

Sensitivity — one-at-a-time (OAT) on the long+lend book

Method. Vary one cost assumption across its range, hold the rest at base, at a fixed 90% and 80% model. This shows which single input the result depends on most — and it is borrow rate (the cost of lending), by a clear margin. (Shortable-fraction and short-executability drop out: no short leg.)

Vary this alone90% model — median [5–95th]80% model — median [5–95th]
Borrow rate (cost of lending)$26.5M [23.0, 30.4]$23.9M [19.8, 29.1]
Utilization$25.6M [22.3, 28.5]$23.0M [19.0, 26.7]
Post-catalyst borrow$26.3M [23.2, 28.4]$23.7M [20.1, 26.9]
Round-trip impact$25.7M [22.8, 27.6]$23.2M [19.1, 26.4]

Read: borrow rate has the widest single-variable spread — it is the one input to nail down. The per-scenario table above (BEAR/BASE/BULL) already shows the combined bad/good-times picture; accuracy is stress-tested in the joint Monte Carlo below.

Accuracy degradation (deployed long+lend): 100% → $28.9M, 90% → $26.3M, 80% → ~$24M — graceful, cushioned by diversification and lending income. Accuracy is the dominant driver, which is why it is analysed on its own axis rather than blended into the Monte Carlo.

Monte Carlo — is this luck or robust?

What "same baseline" means. The result's strongest driver is model accuracy. To compare the two other sources of uncertainty fairly, we pin accuracy at one common value (90%, then 80% as a stress) across all three tests. Any spread you then see is caused only by the thing that test varies — not by accuracy drifting. Concretely: A re-draws which deals you got (deal luck); B1 / B2 re-draw the four cost assumptions below (assumption luck). Without a common baseline, a gap could mean unlucky deals, unlucky costs, or just a worse model — and you couldn't tell which.

Held FIXED (the baseline)Drawn at RANDOM each run — distribution
Model accuracy = 90% (primary) / 80% (stress)Borrow rate — triangular(25%, 100%, 250%/yr)
Position size 5% · per-name cap 10% · gross 150%Utilization — uniform(20%, 60%)
Entry / exit T−20/T+63 · T−10/T+5Post-catalyst borrow — uniform(5%, 25% of rate)
our design choices — not market riskRound-trip impact — uniform(40, 150 bps)

Independent (B1) vs correlated / copula (B2). B1 draws the four at random separately. B2 draws them so they move together: in a bad-liquidity regime borrow gets pricier, utilization falls and impact rises all at once. A Gaussian copula ties the four to one shared "stress" factor. B2 is the realistic, slightly-worse-tail version — the honest one to quote.

median  [90% CI]  P(loss)		80% model
median  [90% CI]  P(loss)
A. Trade luck — bootstrap over deals$26.6M  [20.3, 33.3]  0.0%$23.8M  [17.6, 30.3]  0.0%
B1. Assumption luck — independent$26.9M  [22.2, 33.2]  0.0%$24.5M  [19.8, 30.7]  0.0%

Read: (1) At a fixed accuracy, trade luck ≈ assumption luck — both land ~$27M (90%) / ~$24M (80%) with near-identical spreads. (2) P(lose money) is 0% in every cell — dropping the money-losing short leg removed the downside scenarios. (3) Un-hedged sits ~$3–4M higher at both baselines: the hedge cost return in this window. (4) Caveat: every MC price path is from 2016–2019, so "0% loss" means in a 2016–2019-like market — a sector-wide crash is a separate risk (what the hedge is for). Accuracy remains the dominant lever.

Net read. Deployed long+lend book. Realistic 90%-model version: $26.3M (+163%), CAGR ~27%, Sharpe 1.47, maxDD -18% over 2016-2019 — the number to quote (perfect-foresight ceiling $28.9M). It beats the S&P (+67%) on return and Sharpe. The strategy proves two structural claims — lending is the core alpha (+18% over price-only), and the signal lives only in small-caps. The edge concentrates entirely in failure-class precision; capacity caps it at a sleeve (~$50-150M AUM).

Proposal: separating the full dataset into trial phases

The user's core question — the raw file's stage column mixes phase labels with regulatory-decision labels in one field, with no explicit phase-of-pivotal-trial link for Approved/CRL rows.

What the "Approved or CRL" column actually contains

It's not an outcome column and a phase column layered together by accident — it's a single catalyst-type field with 13 distinct values in the cleaned data:

ValueCountWhat it means
Phase 1 / 1b / 1-2259early readout, not yet pivotal
Phase 2 / 2a / 2b566mid-stage readout
Phase 2/323seamless/adaptive trial readout
Phase 3689pivotal-trial readout
NDA / BLA Filing, PDUFA10regulatory-process milestones, not trial results
Approved513terminal regulatory decision (positive)
CRL120terminal regulatory decision (negative)

Why Approved/CRL already is effectively "post-Phase-3"

FDA approval decisions are made almost entirely on pivotal Phase 3 data (accelerated-approval-off-Phase-2 is the exception, not the rule). So the Approved/CRL slice used above is already a reasonable proxy for "Phase 3 pivotal outcome" — this is the same population the old EDGAR-matched pipeline was trying to approximate at n=47, just reached here directly through a curated regulatory-decision date instead of guessing a trial-completion-to-filing match. That's the main reason this source is a real improvement, not just a different dataset.

Recommended linking scheme, to get an explicit phase per event

  1. Primary (free, no external calls): for every Approved/CRL row, look back within this same CSV for the most recent prior row sharing Ticker + a fuzzy-matched Drug Name (strip parentheticals/trial-name suffixes the same way the PubChem retry step did) whose status is Phase 1/2/3. That row's phase is the pivotal phase. Cheap, deterministic, no rate limits — the same trick that made PubChem name-matching recover 267 of 462 drugs here.
  2. Validation on a sample: cross-check ~30 linked pairs against Drugs@FDA (openFDA, free) by brand/generic name — it returns submission type (NDA/BLA) and approval history but not trial phase directly, so it validates the drug identity match, not the phase itself.
  3. Fallback for unlinked rows: ClinicalTrials.gov search by intervention name + phase=PHASE3 + status Completed, dated before the Approved/CRL catalyst date — same idea as the CTOD/EDGAR pipeline in the other project, but only needed for whatever step 1 can't resolve, which should be a minority.

What this unlocks beyond the Approved/CRL slice done here

The 1,547 Phase 1/1b/1-2/2/2a/2b/2-3/3 rows have no explicit success/failure label — only free-text Catalyst Description ("met its primary endpoint" vs. "did not meet…"). A simple keyword classifier on that text (same result-language approach used for EDGAR filing scoring in the other project) would let mid-phase readouts be priced the same way as Approved/CRL here — extending this analysis to Phase 1/2 catalysts, not just terminal regulatory decisions.
